summary: For 7–8 year olds, connecting representations widens to include the NUMBER LINE, bigger (three-digit) numbers, money/measurement, and fractions. The core objective: move fluently among a real situation, a number line, a bar model, and a symbolic equation, explaining what each part represents and keeping every number tied to its referent (including units). The pivotal new representation is the number line, which shows a fraction as a NUMBER with a magnitude — a length/position — not two whole numbers stacked. The load-bearing misconceptions: placing 3/4 between 3 and 4 (reading numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers), and counting tick marks/parts without seeing that numerator and denominator together name one quantity. The operational equals-sign habit (left-to-right compute; drop units) also persists into multi-step money/measurement sentences. Teaching keeps every symbol tied to its referent and uses partitioning on number lines plus bar models to focus on quantity rather than count of parts.
misconceptions: Places 3/4 between 3 and 4, reading numerator and denominator as two separate whole numbers
Counts tick marks or parts without seeing that numerator and denominator together name one quantity
Partitions with the wrong number of marks (four hash marks for fourths) or treats the whole line as the unit
Keeps the operational equals-sign habit in multi-step money/measurement sentences and drops units off the numbers

activities.title: Place a fraction on a number line as a length
steps: Given a number line that runs 0 to 4, decide where 3/4 belongs before marking it.

If you first place it between 3 and 4, judge how far that point is from 0 — it stretches past 3, far too long for 'three quarters' (an interactive tool can light up this length, but you can equally read the distance on a fixed, accurately drawn line).
Drag or redraw 3/4 back between 0 and 1, partition that first unit into four equal parts, and mark three of those steps from 0.
State the single amount that point names in one sentence (e.g. 'three of four equal parts of one whole, which is less than 1').
Use a whole-number/fraction view to contrast where 3 and 4 sit versus where 3/4 sits.
Extend: place 5/4 and explain how a fraction can be more than 1.
activities.insight: A fraction is a single number with a magnitude — a length/position from 0 — not a numerator and a denominator parked side by side as two whole numbers.

activities.title: Partition an unmarked line and name the quantity
steps: Start from a number line with only its endpoints (0 and 1) marked — no interior tick marks.
Cut the space from 0 to 1 into the number of equal parts needed for the fraction you want (e.g. four parts for fourths).
Say how many marks you had to add between 0 and 1 and why that many (fourths need three interior marks).
Point to the exact spot for the fraction and state what single amount that point represents — do not just count marks.
activities.insight: A point on the line names one quantity; the numerator and denominator together specify a single number, and partitioning into n equal parts needs n−1 interior marks.

activities.title: Build a bar model and equation for a money/measurement story, units attached
steps: Read a measurement or money story, e.g. 'A ribbon is 245 cm long; 3/4 of a metre is cut off.'
Draw a bar model that shows the whole, the parts, and where the unknown sits.
Before combining any numbers, convert so every quantity is in the SAME unit — e.g. 3/4 of a metre = 75 cm — so you are not subtracting 3/4 from 245.

Write a matching equation in which each number keeps its referent and a unit, using the common unit you converted to (for this ribbon, every quantity in cm, e.g. 245 cm − 75 cm = ? cm; use £ or pence consistently when the story is about money).
Say aloud what each number in the equation points back to in the situation, then solve using the bar (245 cm − 75 cm = 170 cm).
Translate in both directions: given an equation, describe the story and draw its bar; given a story, write the equation.
activities.insight: Equations should be structurally faithful to the situation — each number carries a referent and unit, quantities must share a unit before combining, and '=' means 'the same amount as', not 'compute left to right'.

activities.title: Argue it out: where does 3/4 really live?
steps: Respond to a partner (real or in-role) who places 3/4 between 3 and 4, saying 'because it's got a 3 and a 4 in it.'
Say whether you agree, then show and explain where 3/4 really belongs and how you found its exact spot.
Finish a because-clause: 'It goes between 0 and 1 because…'.
Judge a candidate equation the partner proposes for a money problem, and map each number to the story.
Tackle a follow-up — 'Is 3/4 bigger or smaller than 1?', 'Where would 5/4 go?' — to defend your reasoning.
activities.insight: Explaining why 3/4 is not between 3 and 4 — and why the numerator/denominator pair names one magnitude — consolidates the concept and can expose shaky reasoning that a correct-looking placement might hide.

activities.title: Linked worked example: one story, four representations
steps: Study a matched set: a story, its bar model, its number line, and its equation side by side.
Highlight (e.g. tap) one part and see the matching parts in the other representations light up.
For each representation, say what it shows that the others make less visible (magnitude on the line; whole/part structure on the bar; the exact relation in the equation).
Then, without the linked view, reconstruct the bar, line, and equation for a new story yourself.
activities.insight: The four representations describe the same quantities; seeing the correspondences prepares the learner to construct and translate among them independently.

checkQuestion: A classmate is putting fractions on a number line that goes from 0 to 4. They put 3/4 in the space between the 3 and the 4, saying 'because it's got a 3 and a 4 in it.' Do you agree with where they put it? Talk me through where 3/4 really belongs and how you know — and show me how you'd find its exact spot.
checkAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child rejecting the between-3-and-4 placement, treating 3/4 as ONE number with a magnitude less than 1, and locating it by partitioning the unit from 0 to 1 into four equal parts and counting three — explaining that numerator and denominator together name a single quantity, not two whole numbers.
